claim: BMP signaling generates a ventrally-peaking gradient that patterns the dorsal-ventral axis in zebrafish embryos during late blastula and early gastrulation stages.
source: During late blastula and early gastrulation stages in zebrafish embryos, graded transcription and subsequent diffusion of BMP ligands, together with dorsally secreted BMP inhibitors such as Chordin, generate a ventrally-peaking gradient of BMP signaling that patterns the dorsal-ventral axis (Figure 1C; Pomreinke et al., 2017; Zinski et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Pomreinke et al., 2017; Zinski et al., 2017) and references to Figure 1C showing the BMP signaling gradient.

claim: 16 high-confidence BMP target genes were identified that are both upregulated in bmp-overexpressing embryos and downregulated in chordin-overexpressing embryos.
source: We identified 16 high-confidence target genes that are significantly upregulated in bmp-overexpressing embryos and downregulated in embryos overexpressing the BMP inhibitor chordin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D and Supplementary file 1.

claim: BMP target genes have diverse spatial expression patterns along the dorsal-ventral axis at shield stage.
source: We then used fluorescence in situ hybridization and SPIM to quantify the spatial expression profiles of BMP target genes along the dorsal-ventral axis at shield stage (~6.75 hpf) and found that target genes have different expression profiles along this axis (Figure 1F–Y, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Materials and methods; some genes could not be quantified due to weak signal or inability to reliably identify the ventral side).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1F–Y.

claim: BMP target gene spatial expression broadness ranges from 40–100% dorsal-ventral embryo length.
source: Using this definition, spatial gene expression broadness ranges from 40–100% dorsal-ventral embryo length (Figure 1F–Y).
evidence: The claim is based on quantification of spatial expression profiles shown in Figure 1F–Y.

claim: Some BMP target genes are uniformly expressed along the animal-vegetal axis on the ventral side, while others are restricted to or excluded from the margin.
source: Strikingly, pronounced differences along the orthogonal animal-vegetal axis were also evident: Genes were either uniformly expressed along this axis on the ventral side (sizzled, ved, apoc1l, and bambia), restricted to the margin (cdx4 and eve1), or excluded from the margin (foxi1, klf2b, gata2a, and tfap2c) (Figure 1C,F–O').
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence in situ hybridization images shown in Figure 1C,F–O'.

claim: BMP target gene activation times range from 3.4 to 6.3 hours post-fertilization.
source: BMP target gene activation times defined in this way ranged from 3.4 to 6.3 hpf (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is based on NanoString temporal expression data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Opto-BMP reversibly activates BMP signaling in zebrafish embryos in response to blue light exposure.
source: At both stages, Opto-BMP embryos showed a dramatic increase in BMP signaling within 10 min of light exposure, and signaling levels returned to normal after light removal. These experiments demonstrate that Opto-BMP reversibly activates BMP signaling in zebrafish embryos in response to light.
evidence: The claim is supported by pSmad1/5/9 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I,J.

claim: Most BMP target genes are competent to respond to BMP signaling at early developmental stages (high stage, 3.5-4 hpf).
source: While cdx4 is not competent to respond to an early BMP signaling pulse and crabp2b did not clearly respond to either an early or late signaling pulse, all other tested high-confidence BMP target genes responded at high stage. Therefore, differences in competence to respond to BMP signaling at early stages do not explain the majority of diversity in activation timing.
evidence: The claim is based on NanoString data showing transcriptional responses to optogenetic BMP pulses (Figure 4).

claim: Differential transcription kinetics in response to BMP signaling play a minor role in generating distinct spatiotemporal expression patterns of BMP target genes.
source: Together, our analyses indicate that differential transcription kinetics in response to BMP signaling play a minor role in generating the distinct spatiotemporal expression patterns of BMP target genes.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of maximum transcript counts and induction/decay constants shown in Figure 5.

claim: Not all spatiotemporal BMP target gene expression differences are due to different signaling activation thresholds.
source: Our experiments exposing embryos to different amplitude BMP signaling pulses therefore suggest that not all spatiotemporal target gene expression differences are due to different signaling activation thresholds, although a subset may be (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is based on experiments with high- and low-amplitude BMP signaling pulses shown in Figure 6.

claim: FGF inhibition increases the amplitude of the BMP signaling gradient at shield stage.
source: At shield stage, Nodal inhibition did not observably affect BMP signaling (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1F–G'), whereas FGF inhibition increased the amplitude of the BMP signaling gradient (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E').
evidence: The claim is supported by pSmad1/5/9 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E'.

claim: Simultaneous inhibition of both FGF and Nodal signaling increases both the amplitude and spatial broadness of the BMP signaling gradient.
source: Simultaneous inhibition of both FGF and Nodal signaling increased both the amplitude and spatial broadness of the BMP signaling gradient (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1H–J', and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by pSmad1/5/9 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1H–J', and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–K.

claim: FGF and Nodal signaling are responsible for the margin exclusion of some BMP target genes (foxi1, klf2b, gata2a, and tfap2c).
source: The margin exclusion of the BMP target genes foxi1, klf2b, gata2a, and tfap2c can be explained by FGF/Nodal-mediated inhibition (Figure 7K).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence in situ hybridization data showing that margin-excluded genes shift into the margin when FGF and Nodal are inhibited (Figure 7I,L,M, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: Combinatorial FGF and Nodal signaling is a major driver of spatial diversity in BMP target gene expression.
source: Our results identify combinatorial FGF and Nodal signaling as a major driver of spatial diversity in BMP target gene expression.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that spatial diversity in BMP target gene expression collapsed when FGF and Nodal were inhibited (Figure 7F,I,N).

claim: Reduced levels of the secreted BMP inhibitor Chordin in embryos lacking FGF/Nodal signaling contribute to BMP signaling expansion.
source: Reduced levels of the secreted BMP inhibitor Chordin in embryos lacking FGF/Nodal signaling (Figure 7—figure supplement 2ZA) are likely to contribute to this BMP signaling expansion (Varga et al., 2007; Londin et al., 2005; Koshida et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by NanoString data showing reduced chordin expression in FGF/Nodal-inhibited embryos (Figure 7—figure supplement 2ZA) and citations to previous work.

claim: FGF restricts the expression of bmp2b.
source: Additionally, FGF restricts the expression of bmp (Londin et al., 2005; Fürthauer et al., 2004; Fürthauer et al., 1997), and we detected increased bmp2b expression in FGF/Nodal-inhibited embryos (Figure 7—figure supplement 2Z).
evidence: The claim is supported by NanoString data showing increased bmp2b expression in FGF/Nodal-inhibited embryos (Figure 7—figure supplement 2Z) and citations to previous work.

claim: Loss of BMP signaling results in dorsalization, whereas excess BMP signaling produces ventralized embryos.
source: Loss of BMP signaling results in dorsalization, whereas excess BMP signaling produces ventralized embryos (Zinski et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Zinski et al., 2018).

claim: BMP ligands bind and assemble complexes of type I and II receptor serine/threonine kinases, resulting in the phosphorylation of Smad1/5/9 and activation of BMP target genes.
source: BMP ligands bind and assemble complexes of type I and II receptor serine/threonine kinases, resulting in the phosphorylation of the signal transducers Smad1/5/9 and activation of BMP target genes (Figure 1B; Derynck and Budi, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a schematic in Figure 1B and a citation to previous work (Derynck and Budi, 2019).

claim: Four of the 16 high-confidence BMP target genes encode repressors of BMP signaling (bambia, sizzled, smad6a, and smad7).
source: Four of the 16 target genes encode repressors of BMP signaling (bambia, sizzled, smad6a, and smad7) and one encodes bmp4, consistent with roles for negative and positive feedbacks in TGF-β-mediated patterning (Zinski et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on the RNA-sequencing identification of BMP target genes and a citation to previous work (Zinski et al., 2018).

claim: crabp2b and znfl2b have not previously been implicated as BMP targets in zebrafish.
source: 14 of these genes (apoc1l, bambia, bmp4, cdx4, eve1, foxi1, gata2a, id2a, klf2b, smad6a, smad7, sizzled, tfap2c, and ved) are known to be positively regulated by BMP in zebrafish (Kashiwada et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015; Kotkamp et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2013; Das and Crump, 2012; de Pater et al., 2012; Kwon et al., 2010; Li and Cornell, 2007; Poulain et al., 2006; Chong et al., 2005; Davidson et al., 2003; Martyn and Schulte-Merker, 2003; Nissen et al., 2003; Solomon et al., 2003; Yabe et al., 2003; Pogoda and Meyer, 2002; Shimizu et al., 2002; Oates et al., 2001; Tsang et al., 2000; Chin et al., 1997; Nikaido et al., 1997; Hammerschmidt et al., 1996a; Hammerschmidt et al., 1996b; Mullins et al., 1996; Detrich et al., 1995; Joly et al., 1993; Joly et al., 1992), whereas crabp2b (Sharma et al., 2005) and znfl2b (Hogan et al., 2006) have not previously been implicated as BMP targets.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with previous literature and citations.

claim: A ventrally-peaking BMP signaling gradient increases in amplitude over time from 2.75 to 7.25 hpf.
source: Similar to previous studies (Pomreinke et al., 2017; Zinski et al., 2017; Ramel and Hill, 2013; Tucker et al., 2008), we observed a ventrally-peaking BMP signaling gradient that increases in amplitude over time (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by pSmad1/5/9 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D,E and citations to previous work.

claim: Injection of mRNA encoding Opto-BMP into zebrafish embryos at the one-cell stage resulted in strong ventralization in light-reared embryos.
source: Injection of mRNA encoding Opto-BMP into zebrafish embryos at the one-cell stage resulted in strong ventralization in light-reared embryos, consistent with excess BMP signaling, whereas dark-reared siblings were mostly aphenotypic (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,K,L).
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic scoring data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,K,L.

claim: Spatially localized activation of BMP signaling was possible using selective plane illumination microscopy (SPIM).
source: Spatially localized activation of BMP signaling was also possible using SPIM, further demonstrating light-dependent signaling activation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by pSmad1/5/9 immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: cdx4 is not competent to respond to an early BMP signaling pulse at high stage.
source: While cdx4 is not competent to respond to an early BMP signaling pulse and crabp2b did not clearly respond to either an early or late signaling pulse, all other tested high-confidence BMP target genes responded at high stage.
evidence: The claim is based on NanoString data showing transcriptional responses to optogenetic BMP pulses (Figure 4K).

claim: crabp2b did not clearly respond to either an early or late BMP signaling pulse.
source: While cdx4 is not competent to respond to an early BMP signaling pulse and crabp2b did not clearly respond to either an early or late signaling pulse, all other tested high-confidence BMP target genes responded at high stage.
evidence: The claim is based on NanoString data showing transcriptional responses to optogenetic BMP pulses (Figure 4L).

claim: There is a weak negative correlation between maximum transcript counts and activation time in response to a high-stage BMP signaling pulse.
source: However, we observed a weak negative correlation (Figure 5B) or no correlation (Figure 5D) between maximum transcript counts and activation time, and found similar results for range (Figure 5C,E).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There is no correlation between maximum transcript counts and activation time in response to a shield-stage BMP signaling pulse.
source: However, we observed a weak negative correlation (Figure 5B) or no correlation (Figure 5D) between maximum transcript counts and activation time, and found similar results for range (Figure 5C,E).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There is a weak negative correlation between induction constant (σ) and activation time.
source: We found a weak negative correlation between σ and activation time (Figure 5F), and no correlation between σ and range (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: There is no correlation between induction constant (σ) and spatial range.
source: We found a weak negative correlation between σ and activation time (Figure 5F), and no correlation between σ and range (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: There is a strong positive correlation between maximum transcript count and induction constant (σ).
source: In addition, we observed a strong positive correlation between maximum transcript count and σ (Figure 5J), and no correlation between maximum transcript count and λ (Figure 5K), suggesting that production dominates transcription kinetics, and supporting the use of maximum transcript count as a proxy for induction rate.
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 5J.

claim: After a 10 min low-amplitude BMP signaling pulse, foxi1 was significantly activated, whereas broader genes were not robustly induced.
source: However, after a 10 min low-amplitude exposure, the third most narrowly expressed gene, foxi1, was significantly activated, whereas the broader genes were not robustly induced (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is based on NanoString data showing transcriptional responses to low-amplitude BMP pulses (Figure 6C).

claim: A 20 min low-amplitude BMP signaling pulse significantly activated both narrowly and broadly expressed genes.
source: A longer 20 min low-amplitude pulse significantly activated both narrowly and broadly expressed genes (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is based on NanoString data showing transcriptional responses to low-amplitude BMP pulses (Figure 6E).

claim: Nodal inhibition did not detectably alter BMP signaling at shield stage.
source: Loss of Nodal did not detectably alter BMP signaling at shield stage. This is surprising because early expression of fgf is thought to depend on Nodal (van Boxtel et al., 2015; Maegawa et al., 2006; Mathieu et al., 2004; Gritsman et al., 1999; Rodaway et al., 1999), although low levels of fgf3 appear to be present at late blastula stages in Nodal signaling mutants (Mathieu et al., 2004), and weak FGF activity is detectable in Nodal inhibitor-treated embryos (van Boxtel et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on pSmad1/5/9 immunofluorescence data (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1F–G') and citations to previous work.

claim: Nodal is responsible for the dorsal expression of the BMP target gene apoc1l.
source: Nodal is also responsible for the dorsal expression of the BMP target gene apoc1l (Figure 1O,O',Y), which is lost in the absence of Nodal (Figure 7H, Figure 7—figure supplement 1N, and Figure 7—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is based on fluorescence in situ hybridization data showing loss of apoc1l dorsal expression in Nodal-inhibited embryos (Figure 7H, Figure 7—figure supplement 1N, and Figure 7—figure supplement 3C).

claim: Excess BMP signaling at the margin in embryos lacking FGF and Nodal does not explain the observed gene expression shifts of margin-excluded genes.
source: Excess BMP signaling at the margin in embryos lacking FGF and Nodal (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1H–J', and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–K) does not explain the observed gene expression shifts because no shifts were evident in bmp-overexpressing embryos (Figure 7J,L,M, Figure 7—figure supplement 1L,P, and Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of fluorescence in situ hybridization data between FGF/Nodal-inhibited and bmp-overexpressing embryos.

claim: FGF and Nodal do not contribute to diversity in BMP target gene activation timing.
source: Although transcript levels of several BMP targets were higher in treated compared to untreated embryos at later stages, their activation times were still diverse, suggesting that inputs other than FGF and Nodal are responsible for differences in activation times.
evidence: The claim is based on NanoString temporal expression data in FGF/Nodal-inhibited embryos (Figure 7—figure supplement 2L–Y).

claim: Embryos lacking both FGF and Nodal had lower spatial coefficients of variation at almost all positions along the dorsal-ventral axis compared to untreated embryos.
source: Strikingly, embryos lacking both FGF and Nodal had lower coefficients of variation at almost all positions along the dorsal-ventral axis compared to untreated embryos (Figure 7N).
evidence: The claim is based on calculation of spatial coefficients of variation shown in Figure 7N.

claim: Most embryos experiencing transient activation of BMP signaling lack gross morphological defects.
source: For example, most embryos experiencing transient activation of BMP signaling lack gross morphological defects (Figure 3C–E, Figure 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,K,L, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on phenotypic observations from optogenetic experiments shown in multiple figures.

claim: Five out of 16 high-confidence BMP target genes affect BMP signaling.
source: Together with previous work (reviewed in Zinski et al., 2018), several of our observations indicate that feedback is an important feature of the BMP patterning system: Five out of 16 high-confidence BMP target genes affect BMP signaling (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and embryos can experience a dip in signaling levels after a signaling pulse (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: The claim is based on the RNA-sequencing identification of BMP target genes shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Embryos can experience a dip in BMP signaling levels after an optogenetic BMP signaling pulse.
source: Together with previous work (reviewed in Zinski et al., 2018), several of our observations indicate that feedback is an important feature of the BMP patterning system: Five out of 16 high-confidence BMP target genes affect BMP signaling (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and embryos can experience a dip in signaling levels after a signaling pulse (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: The claim is based on pSmad1/5/9 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1J.

claim: The restriction of eve1 and cdx4 to the margin is not explained by FGF or Nodal signaling.
source: Consistent with previous work (Swanhart et al., 2010; Ota et al., 2009; Bennett et al., 2007; Ho et al., 2006; Londin et al., 2005; Shimizu et al., 2005; Rentzsch et al., 2004), in the absence of FGF or Nodal, eve1 and cdx4 were still expressed at the ventral margin (Figure 7—figure supplement 1; we note, however, conflicting reports with dominant-negative FGF receptors [Ota et al., 2009; Kudoh et al., 2004; Griffin et al., 1995]).
evidence: The claim is based on fluorescence in situ hybridization data in FGF/Nodal-inhibited embryos (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and citations to previous work.

claim: The temporal expression of eve1 and cdx4 was not significantly affected by loss of FGF/Nodal signaling.
source: FGF and Nodal have no obvious roles in regulating their activation timing or competence since their temporal expression was not significantly affected by loss of FGF/Nodal signaling (Figure 7—figure supplement 2Q,U).
evidence: The claim is based on NanoString temporal expression data in FGF/Nodal-inhibited embryos (Figure 7—figure supplement 2Q,U).

claim: A subset of three genes (sizzled, ved, and bambia) show a monotonically decreasing relationship between range and activation time.
source: We note that a subset of three genes (sizzled, ved, and bambia) that are neither restricted to nor excluded from the margin do show a monotonically decreasing relationship between range and activation time (Figure 2O) as well as activation dynamics that could be roughly commensurate with signaling input (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), consistent with the gradient threshold model.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of spatial and temporal expression data shown in Figure 2O and Figure 6C.
